what_its_for: Elotuzumab is a cancer medicine used to treat multiple myeloma, which is a type of blood cancer. It is always used together with other cancer medicines (such as lenalidomide and dexamethasone, or pomalidomide and dexamethasone). It works by helping your immune system find and attack cancer cells.
how_to_take: Elotuzumab is given as an intravenous (IV) infusion, meaning it is slowly dripped into your vein through a needle or catheter at a clinic or hospital. A healthcare provider will give you this medicine — you will NOT give it to yourself at home. Before each infusion, you will receive pre-medications (such as antihistamines, steroids, and acetaminophen) to help prevent infusion reactions. The infusion can take several hours, so plan your day accordingly. Do not miss any scheduled appointments.
dosing: Your doctor will decide the exact dose based on your body weight and the treatment combination being used. Elotuzumab is typically given once a week for the first two cycles (about 8 weeks), and then every two weeks or once a month after that. Each cycle is 28 days long. Always follow your doctor's specific schedule. Never change your dose or schedule on your own.
missed_dose: Because this medicine is given by a healthcare provider at a clinic, missing a dose means missing your scheduled appointment. If you need to reschedule or if you miss an appointment, call your doctor or cancer care team right away. Do not try to double up doses or change your schedule without talking to your doctor first.
storage: You will not store this medicine at home — it is prepared and stored by healthcare professionals at your treatment center. However, if you are given any pre-medications to take at home before your infusion, store those medicines as directed on their labels, usually at room temperature and away from heat, light, and moisture. Keep all medicines out of reach of children.
what_to_avoid: Avoid live vaccines (such as shingles vaccine or nasal flu spray) while on this treatment unless your doctor specifically approves them. Avoid people who are sick with infections such as colds or flu, as your immune system may be weakened. Avoid grapefruit and grapefruit juice if you are also taking certain other medicines — ask your pharmacist. Do not drive or operate heavy machinery right after your infusion if you feel dizzy or tired from the pre-medications.
when_to_call_doctor: Call your doctor or go to the emergency room right away if you have: a fever of 100.4°F (38°C) or higher, chills, or signs of infection; trouble breathing, chest tightness, or wheezing during or after an infusion; severe skin rash, itching, or hives; unusual bleeding or bruising; feeling very tired or weak; numbness or tingling in hands or feet; signs of liver problems such as yellowing of the skin or eyes, dark urine, or stomach pain; or any new or worsening symptoms. Also tell your doctor if you feel faint, have a fast heartbeat, or feel your face flushing during an infusion.
when_it_works: Elotuzumab starts working right away in your body, but it may take several weeks or months before you or your doctor notice improvement in your condition through lab tests or how you feel. Every patient is different. Your doctor will monitor your progress with regular blood tests and check-ups. Do not stop treatment because you do not feel immediate results — continue going to all your scheduled appointments.
special_populations: Pregnancy: This medicine may harm an unborn baby. Women who can become pregnant should use effective birth control during treatment and for 6 months after the last dose. Tell your doctor right away if you become pregnant. Breastfeeding: It is not known if elotuzumab passes into breast milk. Do not breastfeed while taking this medicine. Men: Male patients with female partners who could become pregnant should also use birth control during treatment and for 6 months after the last dose. Elderly patients (65 and older): Elderly patients can receive this medicine, but they may need closer monitoring for side effects. Kidney or liver problems: Tell your doctor about any kidney or liver issues before starting treatment, as your doctor will monitor you carefully.
